---
title: "Nonuniform grids"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using ConvolutionInterpolations, CairoMakie, Printf
```

On a uniform grid every kernel copy is the same polynomial, shifted. On a nonuniform grid the
spacing changes from interval to interval, and the Julia package carries a second family of
kernels whose polynomial pieces are recomputed for the actual knots, so that the interpolant
keeps its cardinality and its polynomial reproduction on any strictly increasing knot vector.
Nothing needs to be switched on: passing knots that are not uniformly spaced selects them.

The Python port works on uniform grids only, so far; the [feature matrix](../features.qmd)
tracks the port.

## The kernels

Two kinds of nonuniform kernel are available:

- `:n3` is the nonuniform cubic, the counterpart of `:a3`: closed-form weights, a four-wide
  stencil and no precomputation, so it costs about what the uniform cubic costs. It is the
  default on nonuniform grids.
- `:b5` to `:b13` are the nonuniform counterparts of the high-order kernels. They converge at
  order degree + 1 — `:b5` at 6th order and `:b13` at 14th — and provide derivatives up to 7th
  order. Their weights are projected onto each interval in exact rational arithmetic when the
  interpolant is built, so construction costs one projection per interval and grows with the
  number of intervals; evaluation is as local as on a uniform grid.

The uniform `:a` kernels other than `:a3` have no nonuniform counterpart.

## A first example

A damped sine sampled on a grid that is dense where the function varies fast and sparse where
it has settled, interpolated with `:b7` and differentiated twice:

```{julia}
x = [0.0, 0.15, 0.4, 0.7, 1.5, 2.5, 3.8, 4.2, 4.6, 4.8, 5.0,
     5.3, 5.6, 6.0, 6.5, 7.0, 7.3, 7.8, 8.2, 8.5, 9.0, 9.5, 10.0]   # an irregular knot vector
f(x) = sin(x) * exp(-x / 5)                               # the function being sampled
y = f.(x)                                                 # the values at the knots

itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7)       # nonuniform grid detected from the knots
d1 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7, derivative = 1)   # its first derivative
d2 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7, derivative = 2)   # its second derivative

xf = range(0, 10, length = 600)                           # fine points for plotting
fig = Figure(size = (800, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x")
lines!(ax, xf, itp.(xf); label = "interpolant")
lines!(ax, xf, d1.(xf); label = "first derivative")
lines!(ax, xf, d2.(xf); label = "second derivative")
lines!(ax, xf, f.(xf); color = :black, label = "f")
scatter!(ax, x, y; markersize = 10, color = :white, strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1.5, label = "knots")
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
df(x) = exp(-x / 5) * (cos(x) - sin(x) / 5)               # the exact first derivative
println("| at x = 2.9 (a sparse part of the grid) | f | f′ |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| interpolant | %.10f | %.10f |\n", itp(2.9), d1(2.9))
@printf("| exact | %.10f | %.10f |\n", f(2.9), df(2.9))
```

## Convergence on a graded grid

The orders hold on nonuniform grids as they do on uniform ones. Here the knots are a uniform
grid pushed through a smooth monotone map, so that each refinement keeps the grading and halves
every spacing, and Runge's function is interpolated with four kernels:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The convergence study"
runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2)                                # Runge's function
grade(u) = u + 0.3 * sin(π * u) / π                       # a monotone map of [−1, 1] onto itself, dense near the centre
xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001)                          # fine points for measuring the error
kernels = (:n3, :b5, :b7, :b9, :b11)
ns = [41, 81, 161, 321, 641]                              # the numbers of knots
hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1)                                       # the spacings of the uniform grid before grading

errors = [begin
              xn = grade.(range(-1, 1, length = n))       # the graded knots
              itp_k = convolution_interpolation(xn, runge.(xn); kernel = k)
              maximum(abs.(itp_k.(xr) .- runge.(xr)))
          end for n in ns, k in kernels]

fig = Figure(size = (800, 420))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true,
          xlabel = "mean spacing h", ylabel = "largest error")
for (j, k) in enumerate(kernels)
    scatterlines!(ax, hs, max.(errors[:, j], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = string(k))
end
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
observed = [begin
                e = errors[:, j]
                i = findlast(v -> v > 1e-11, e); i = max(i, 2)   # the finest grid still clear of rounding
                log(e[i-1] / e[i]) / log(hs[i-1] / hs[i])
            end for j in eachindex(kernels)]
println("| | ", join(("`$k`" for k in kernels), " | "), " |")
println("|:--|", "--:|"^length(kernels))
println("| observed convergence order | ", join((@sprintf("%.2f", o) for o in observed), " | "), " |")
```

## In more dimensions

Nonuniform knots can be given per axis, and the grid is the tensor product of the axes, so a
log-spaced axis and a uniform axis combine freely. Each axis chooses its own kernel and
derivative order:

```{julia}
xg = 10 .^ range(-2, 0, length = 25)                      # a log-spaced axis on [0.01, 1]
yg = range(0, 1, length = 20)                             # a uniform axis
data = [log(xi) * cos(π * yi) for xi in xg, yi in yg]     # log(x)·cos(πy) on the grid

itp2 = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; kernel = :b7)                       # interpolation
dx2 = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; kernel = (:b7, :b5), derivative = (1, 0))  # ∂/∂x, two kernels

itp2(0.05, 0.3), dx2(0.05, 0.3)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| at (0.05, 0.3) | f | ∂f/∂x |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| interpolant | %.10f | %.10f |\n", itp2(0.05, 0.3), dx2(0.05, 0.3))
@printf("| exact | %.10f | %.10f |\n", log(0.05) * cos(0.3π), cos(0.3π) / 0.05)
```

The precomputation of the `:b` kernels is per interval and per axis, so it stays cheap on a
tensor-product grid: a 1000 × 1000 grid needs two thousand projections, not a million.

## What is not available

Antiderivatives are uniform-grid only: the precomputed tails that make an integral cost the
same as an interpolation rely on equal spacing. To integrate data on a nonuniform grid,
evaluate the nonuniform interpolant on a uniform grid fine enough to carry it and integrate
that with `derivative = -1`, as on the [integrals page](integrals.qmd). Lazy construction, for
large grids, is available with `:n3` only; the `:b` kernels build their ghost values when the
interpolant is created.
